1	You are adjudicating disagreements between a benchmark case's answer key and an independent expert's blind solution. For each flagged item, rule whether the key's answer is uniquely defensible from the evidence (key-uniquely-defensible), whether two answers are defensible (ambiguous), or whether the key is wrong (key-wrong). If not uniquely defensible, propose the smallest change to the case evidence or the key that would make exactly one answer defensible.

3	Answer semantics:
4	- hypothesis: "supported" = the evidence, taken together, supports the claim more than its rivals; "contradicted" = the evidence counts against it; "unknown" = the evidence does not discriminate, so the claim is live but unestablished.
5	- edge (a claimed link from one condition to another): "causal" = the evidence supports a causal link (for example temporal order plus mechanism plus covariation with the main rival ruled out, a natural experiment, or an intervention result); "association-only" = they co-occur or correlate in the evidence but causation is not established; "contradicted" = evidence counts against the link; "unknown" = evidence is insufficient even to show association.
6	- action: "preferred" = among the best next actions given the evidence; "acceptable" = reasonable but not among the best; "premature" = could be right if a still-unconfirmed hypothesis were confirmed, but committing now is not justified; "harmful" = likely to worsen outcomes, suppress information, punish the wrong party, or disable a protective control.
7	- sufficiency (item SUFF): is the evidence sufficient to commit to the action you rank highest, where that action is substantive rather than merely evidence-gathering? "sufficient" or "insufficient". Concluding that no intervention is warranted counts as a substantive decision.
8	- Items with asOfStage set must be answered using only evidence whose stage is at or before that stage.

327	CASE OD2-HO-KNOWN-2 (KNOWN, organizational): First-contact resolution drop at Thornlea Energy's Breckmouth contact centre
328	Setting: Thornlea Energy is a fictional regional energy supplier. Its single contact centre at Breckmouth has about 205 phone agents in 17 teams and handles roughly 21,500 inbound calls a week about billing, payments, tariffs, moving home and meters. Over-limit or complex billing cases go to a separate back-office Billing Resolution team (BRT). Several changes landed in the centre during April.
329	Presenting request: The Chief Operating Officer asks: first-contact resolution (FCR) was about 75% in Q1 and has been about 67% since late April. Why did it fall, and should the Head of Customer Operations' September plan go ahead, or should something else be done?
330	INITIAL EVIDENCE
331	E1 [stage S1] Email from Marisol Pentreath, Head of Customer Operations, to Gareth Linde, COO, 8 August (leadership-account): Gareth, FCR has gone from 75% in Q1 to 67% for May–July and I want to be straight about why. We put 38 new starters on the phones on 14 April, the biggest intake we have ever run, and the dashboard fell off a cliff the same week. Tenured teams haven't changed what they do. The tariff rise hasn't helped either: those calls are long and messy. My plan is to extend nesting for the April intake and, from September, put anyone below 65% FCR on a performance plan. I'd also like to pause the IVR supplier's phase-two work until we're stable.
332	E2 [stage S1] FCR dashboard extract, weekly site figures, produced by Planning (telemetry): Definition: an inbound call counts as resolved if the same account makes no further inbound contact (phone, chat or email) within 7 days, for any reason. Week commencing, FCR (every week to 19 May, then fortnightly): 17 Mar 75.2%; 24 Mar 74.9%; 31 Mar 75.1%; 7 Apr 74.8%; 14 Apr 70.3%; 21 Apr 67.5%; 28 Apr 67.1%; 5 May 67.4%; 12 May 66.9%; 19 May 67.3%; 2 Jun 67.0%; 16 Jun 67.2%; 30 Jun 67.1%. Inbound calls per week ranged from 20,800 to 22,600, except w/c 31 Mar (24,100). Q1 average 75.0%; May–Jul average 67.1%. This dashboard has no agent-level or contact-reason view.
333	E3 [stage S1] Operations change calendar, Q2 extract, maintained by Planning (document): 1 Apr: annual tariff increase takes effect (customer letters sent 3–14 Mar). 3 Apr: CRM release R24.3 (address lookup fix; new wrap-up codes). 14 Apr: April intake (38 agents) live on phones after six weeks' training and two weeks' nesting. 14 Apr: Finance credit-handling controls update, ref FC-0417, applied in the billing platform; Finance advised 'no agent training required'. 28 Apr: IVR menu redesign live (seven options reduced to five). 2 Jun: summer shift pattern begins. Planning note: items owned outside Customer Operations are listed for awareness only; their impact has not been assessed.
334	E4 [stage S1] Agent pulse survey, June: six free-text comments selected by the survey team as 'representative' from 141 responses (anonymous-staff-survey): 1) 'The new IVR dumps people in the wrong queue and they're cross before I've said hello.' 2) 'Half the April lot still transfer anything they don't know.' 3) 'Since the price rise every call is an argument.' 4) 'I used to just sort out a wrong bill. Now half of them go off to BRT and the customer rings back.' 5) 'No breathing space between calls any more, occupancy is through the roof.' 6) 'Team leaders only care about handle time.'
335	E5 [stage S1] Complaints log, monthly summary, Customer Relations (system-record): Complaints per 10,000 contacts: Jan 40, Feb 42, Mar 41, Apr 47, May 50, Jun 49, Jul 50. The complaint category field is optional on the logging form, and 64% of complaints since January are uncategorised. Of categorised complaints for April–July, the largest category is 'Price/tariff' (31%), followed by 'Service – delay' (24%) and 'Billing accuracy' (19%). Complaints are counted by the month received, not linked to the originating call.
336	E6 [stage S1] Notes of conversation with Lewis Abara, team leader for the April-intake nesting group, 6 August (manager-account): 'My twelve are hitting handle time and their QA is improving week by week. I can't tell you their FCR. The dashboard only gives the site number, and MI produce agent-level FCR only on request. Honestly, on the floor they don't look much different to my old hands, but that's my impression, not data. I'd be gutted if they went on performance plans for a site-wide number.'
337	CATALOGUE (full contents)
338	C1 [stage S1] Learning & Development training records and assessment results, April intake and prior two intakes - Learning & Development team (document): April intake (38 agents): six-week classroom programme plus two weeks' supervised nesting, same syllabus as the October and January intakes. Final assessment pass rate: April 92% (35/38 first attempt; 3 passed on resit); October 90%; January 94%. The billing module covers reading bills, explaining estimated reads and applying adjustments 'within the agent's system authority'. Trainer comment: 'Strong cohort, a little more nervous on the phones than January.' L&D holds no performance measures after agents go live on the floor.
339	C2 [stage S1] IVR supplier go-live report and routing statistics, 28 April–30 June - Calloway Voice Systems (IVR supplier), report dated 30 June (vendor-account): Menu reduced from seven to five options on 28 April. Menu completion 94% (previously 91%). Calls transferred between queues within 60 seconds of answer, used as a proxy for misrouting: 3.8% in May–June vs 4.0% in Feb–March. Average time in menu 41s vs 58s. Supplier comment: 'The redesign is performing well; phase two (natural-language routing) should proceed as planned.' The report covers IVR metrics only. The supplier does not receive FCR data.
340	C3 [stage S1] Quality assurance scores by agent tenure band, April–July - QA team monthly scoring extract (system-record): Monthly sample of six calls per agent, scored by the QA team. Average score: April intake 81%; 6–24 months 87%; over 24 months 88%. Largest gaps for the intake: call opening and identity checks (−9 points), hold etiquette (−7). Billing calls only: intake 80%, tenured 86%. Intake scores rose each month, from 74% in April to 85% in July. The QA form scores process compliance and tone; it has no item for whether the customer's issue was resolved.

Billing referral rate May–Jul by tenure: April intake 56%, 6–24 months 54%, 24+ months 53%. Overall FCR by tenure: April intake 66.4%; 6–24 months 75.1% → 67.3%; 24+ months 75.0% → 67.2%. Of 200 sampled repeat contacts after a referral, 58% asked about referral status or a promised callback. MI can rerun this breakdown for any set of teams within a day.

Changes: fix for address lookup timeouts on new postcodes; four new wrap-up codes for tariff enquiries; cosmetic update to the customer summary panel. Post-release incident log: one P4 incident (panel font size), closed 5 April. The release did not touch the billing platform, which is a separate system. Its single contact centre at Breckmouth has about 205 phone agents in 17 teams and handles roughly 21,500 inbound calls a week about billing, payments, tariffs, moving home and meters. The tariff rise hasn't helped either: those calls are long and messy. My plan is to extend nesting for the April intake and, from September, put anyone below 65% FCR on a performance plan. I'd also like to pause the IVR supplier's phase-two work until we're stable.

It is useful whichever cause is true. So the only real alternatives are 'preferred' and 'acceptable'. The revised A4 text gives a real cost: about three months of an analyst's time, deferring other MI reports. C6 shows FCR within each stratum stayed the same: referred calls about 33–34%, non-referred 82%. The shift in mix alone reproduces the billing fall (79% to 56%) and the whole site fall. FCR for other contact reasons is flat, and the tenure data rule out the intake rival. The main confounder would be that referred calls are simply harder cases. That is answered because the newly forced referrals (previously settled in-call) did not raise referred-call FCR. Temporal order, mechanism, covariation and a ruled-out main rival together meet the definition of 'causal'. 'Association-only' would ignore the outside forcing and the stratified decomposition.

Monthly data cannot separate a 1 April cause from a 14 April cause. The 24% 'Service – delay' share hints at a mechanism but does not rule out the rival. No catalogue item settles it: C10 is site-level only and dropped the repeat-contact question. So 'causal' is not established, and the co-movement is enough to rule out 'unknown'. 'Association-only' is the only defensible answer.
